risk_rationale: The 10Y yield has surged 57bp to 4.99%, compressing the term premium and tightening financial conditions materially, while NFP collapsed to 29K — a deterioration of 86K from the prior read — signaling rapid labor market deceleration. WTI at $103.4 and Brent at $123.1 sustain stagflationary pressure, keeping headline CPI at 3.7% and core PCE at 3.0%, well above the Fed's 2% target with no clear disinflation catalyst.
outlook_headline: Stagflation risk is no longer theoretical — slowing growth, sticky inflation, and surging rates are converging simultaneously.
outlook_body: The macro backdrop has deteriorated sharply: a 29K NFP print alongside a 4.2% unemployment rate and 7.6% U-6 signals the labor market is cracking faster than lagging indicators have acknowledged. The 10Y at 4.99% with a 30Y mortgage at 7.32% is delivering a severe demand shock to rate-sensitive sectors, particularly housing, while oil prices sustain cost-push inflation that the Fed cannot address through demand destruction alone. Real GDP at 2.2% annualized provides a thin buffer, but the trajectory is clearly decelerating given the simultaneous tightening of credit, housing, and labor conditions. Portfolio positioning should lean defensive; the risk of a hard landing has risen materially.

tabs.gdp: Real GDP growth of 2.2% annualized provides a deceptively stable headline, but the composition and trajectory matter more than the level at this stage of the cycle. The simultaneous shock of a 57bp rate surge, 29K NFP, and 7.32% mortgage rates will transmit into Q4 and Q1 2027 data with meaningful negative multiplier effects on consumption, residential investment, and business capex. Downside risk to sub-1% growth in the next two quarters is material and rising.
tabs.jobs: A 29K NFP print — down 86K from the prior reading — is a hard stop signal; this is not noise, it is a trend break that warrants immediate reassessment of the soft-landing thesis. Wage growth at 3.9% YoY remains above levels consistent with 2% inflation, but decelerating payrolls will compress aggregate income growth and consumer spending capacity in coming quarters. Leading indicators embedded in this report are unambiguously negative; the labor market is transitioning from resilient to fragile.
tabs.unemp: U-3 unemployment at 4.2% has not yet reached recessionary thresholds, but the 7.6% U-6 reading reveals significant underemployment and labor market slack that the headline rate obscures. The 360bp gap between U-6 and U-3 indicates that part-time-for-economic-reasons and marginally attached workers are accumulating, a pattern consistent with late-cycle deterioration. If NFP continues printing sub-50K, U-3 will breach 4.5% within two to three months, triggering Sahm Rule proximity concerns.
tabs.wages: Wages at 3.9% YoY remain above the Fed's implicit ~3.0-3.5% comfort zone for a 2% inflation target, but the real wage gain against CPI of 3.7% is essentially zero (+0.2pp). Workers are not accumulating real purchasing power, which constrains consumption durability even as nominal wages look resilient. The wage-price spiral risk is diminishing, but wages are not decelerating fast enough to give the Fed confidence to ease.
tabs.cpi: Headline CPI at 3.7% YoY remains 170bp above the Fed's target, driven in large part by energy pass-through from WTI at $103.4, while core CPI at 2.6% shows that underlying disinflation is progressing but incomplete. The divergence between headline and core is a policy trap: the Fed cannot ignore 3.7% headline politically, but core at 2.6% does not justify further aggressive tightening into a deteriorating labor market. Until energy prices correct materially, headline CPI will remain a constraint on any dovish pivot.
tabs.pce: Core PCE at 3.0% is the Fed's primary target metric and remains 100bp above the 2% mandate, confirming that the disinflation process has stalled at an uncomfortable level. The 4.1% personal saving rate is low by historical standards, indicating consumers are drawing down buffers to sustain spending — a dynamic that is unsustainable if labor income growth decelerates sharply from the 29K NFP trajectory. PCE at 3.4% headline combined with a thin saving cushion sets up a consumer spending cliff if employment conditions worsen further.
tabs.yield: The 10Y yield's 57bp surge to 4.99% is the dominant financial conditions shock in this snapshot, pushing the 10Y-2Y spread to a still-narrow 29bp and signaling that term premium is being repriced aggressively. With Fed Funds at 3.88%, the long end is now trading well above the policy rate, reflecting either fiscal supply concerns, inflation re-acceleration fears, or both. The Fed faces a credibility bind: cutting into 3.7% CPI risks unanchoring expectations, while holding or hiking into a 29K NFP environment accelerates the growth slowdown.
tabs.credit: IG OAS at 88bp and HY OAS at 318bp remain relatively contained given the macro deterioration, suggesting credit markets have not yet fully priced the labor market and rate shock visible in other indicators. HY at 318bp is not distressed, but with the 10Y at 4.99% and NFP at 29K, all-in HY yields are approaching levels that will materially impair refinancing for lower-rated issuers. A spread widening episode is a high-probability outcome if the labor deterioration continues; current levels represent complacency risk.
tabs.housing: The 30Y mortgage rate at 7.32% — up 95bp from the prior snapshot — is a severe affordability shock that effectively locks existing homeowners in place and prices marginal buyers out of the market. Housing starts at 1,221K show the supply side is still active, but demand destruction at 7.32% mortgage rates will erode builder confidence and starts data with a 2-3 month lag. The Case-Shiller HPI rising 2.09% YoY (up 143bp) reflects inventory scarcity, not demand strength — a distinction that will invert sharply if rates remain at current levels.
tabs.oil: WTI fell $6.39 to $103.4 but remains acutely elevated, and the $19.7 Brent-WTI spread at $123.1 signals severe international supply tightness that domestic production cannot offset. At these levels, energy costs are a persistent tax on consumer disposable income and corporate margins, sustaining headline CPI above 3.5% regardless of demand-side cooling. The macro transmission risk is stagflationary: oil is simultaneously suppressing real purchasing power and preventing the Fed from pivoting dovish.
tabs.banks: Bank NII faces a complex environment: the 10Y at 4.99% supports asset yields, but a 29K NFP print and rising U-6 at 7.6% are early warning signals for credit quality deterioration in consumer and SME loan books. Credit card delinquencies at 2.9% are elevated and will trend higher if the labor market continues to weaken, compressing reserve release optionality and pressuring earnings guidance. Deposit repricing pressure persists with Fed Funds at 3.88%, and any growth slowdown will reduce loan demand, creating a revenue headwind that offsets the rate tailwind.

signal_flags.note: A 57bp surge in the 10Y is a major financial conditions tightening event; at 4.99% it is approaching the psychologically and technically significant 5% level, which historically triggers risk-off repositioning across equities and credit.

Despite the $6.39 pullback, WTI above $100 sustains stagflationary dynamics. The Brent-WTI spread of $19.7 signals acute global supply stress; any reversal of the WTI decline would push headline CPI materially higher and eliminate remaining Fed flexibility.

A 95bp jump in the 30Y mortgage rate is one of the largest single-snapshot moves on record for this series; at 7.32%, housing affordability is at multi-decade lows and will mechanically suppress transaction volumes, new construction demand, and household wealth effects.

A drop of 86K in monthly payroll additions to just 29K is a threshold-crossing deterioration. Sub-50K NFP prints have historically preceded recession calls within 2-3 quarters; this single data point materially shifts the probability distribution toward hard landing.
